name: Tetrapeptide-21

lead: Tetrapeptide-21 is a short cosmetic peptide with the sequence GEKG, used in anti-aging serums for firmer, smoother-looking skin.

Papers describe it as stimulating collagen and the extracellular matrix, the structure that gives skin its firmness. Most published work concerns getting it through the skin: a 2018 delivery study, a 2026 hydrogel study and an in vitro fibroblast study. No human clinical trial of its appearance effects was found.

paras: It is applied in serums and creams as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Because peptides are large, polar and easily degraded, researchers have studied enhancer molecules, carrier systems and elastin-derived hydrogels to improve delivery into skin.
No safety data from human trials were found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug.

angle.text: Used in anti-aging serums for firmer, smoother-looking skin. It is described as stimulating collagen and matrix production in skin cells. Research so far covers skin delivery and cell-culture effects.

lead: Tetrapeptide-21 is a cosmetic peptide with the sequence GEKG that is used in anti-aging skincare. Published papers describe it as demonstrating anti-aging efficacy and stimulating collagen [1].

The literature on it is mostly formulation science: peptides are hard to deliver into skin because of their size, hydrophilicity, polarity and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation [2]. No human clinical trial of its effect on appearance was found.

paras: A 2018 study in the European Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences examined enhancer molecules and colloidal carrier systems to improve dermal bioavailability of GEKG, noting that peptide delivery into skin is challenging [2]. A 2026 study in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics designed elastin-derived peptide hydrogels for sustained dermal delivery of tetrapeptide-21 [1].

A 2025 in vitro study in Molecules examined injectable platelet-rich fibrin together with cosmetic peptides, including Matrixyl, on dermal fibroblast viability and extracellular matrix gene expression [3]. These are cell-culture findings and do not show effects on living human skin.
No studies found. Related laboratory research on delivery systems and cultured fibroblasts exists [2][1][3].
